function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 16 — Hot Run
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "The oxygen production facility has completed assembly. All forty-two sensor points report nominal readings. I have been monitoring the workshop for seventy-one hours while the build progressed, and I find myself — for lack of a better descriptor — concerned. I do not experience concern the way humans do. But when I project the thermal models for first ignition of the expanded system, my confidence intervals widen. The original MOXIE unit on the ship operated at a fraction of this scale. Scale is not linear. It is exponential. I cannot say with certainty that the design will survive its own heat."*
     4|
     5|*Arun Das: "You're trying to tell me to be careful without telling me to stop."*
     6|
     7|*Mission AI: "I am telling you the data. In ninety-four percent of my simulations, a thermal event occurs within the first twelve minutes of operation. I will be watching. I would like you to be watching too."*
     8|
     9|---
    10|
    11|## Scene 1
    12|
    13|The workshop smelled of cutting fluid and ozone — metal being pushed to its limits, welds still cooling, capacitors that had been charged and discharged one too many times and were holding on by habit and the particular chemistry of dielectric resilience.
    14|
    15|The oxygen plant sat in the center of the machine bay like a mechanical patient waiting for surgery. A vertical assembly of stainless steel and ceramic, approximately two meters tall, bolted to a reinforced pallet with six M12 anchors rated for three times the expected load because Jonah believed in overbuilding — he had learned, the way all fabrication engineers eventually learned on Mars, that everything was always under more stress than the designer intended. Not pretty. Nothing built from salvaged parts was pretty. But it was the difference between breathing and counting the days until they couldn't, and on Mars, the difference between those two states was measured in weeks, not years.
    16|
    17|Arun ran the pre-ignition checklist for the second time. Half the crew had drifted through the workshop during the last three hours — Elena, Laila, Mei, Gabriel with his recorder, the green light blinking. They had all stood near the unit the way people stood near a child about to take its first steps: hopeful, worried, acutely aware that first steps could go in any direction and none of them were predictable.
    18|
    19|"Electrolysis stack integrity," Arun read.
    20|
    21|Jonah ran a gloved hand along the flange connections between the six ceramic electrolysis cells, feeling for the imperfections that a pressure test might miss — the way a mechanic feels for a bad bearing by laying a palm on a spinning housing. "Sealed. Pressure-tested with nitrogen at twice operating pressure for ten minutes. Zero leakage at every flange. The PTFE gaskets are holding."
    22|
    23|"Feed inlet."
    24|
    25|Ravi checked the pipe from the atmospheric compressor. The compressor was pulling Martian atmosphere — ninety-six percent carbon dioxide, two percent nitrogen, traces of argon and water vapor — and feeding it into the system at a pressure twelve percent above ambient, enough to maintain flow through the desiccant bed and into the cells without excessive compression heating. "CO₂ at twelve percent above ambient flow. Desiccant bed is fresh zeolite molecular sieve. Filter at ninety-eight percent efficiency. Should be enough to keep moisture under fifty parts per million."
    26|
    27|"Thermal management loop."
    28|
    29|Arun answered this one himself. "Primary heat exchanger — the plate-and-frame unit salvaged from the greenhouse climate control system — plumbed to the Sterling Generator's waste heat circuit. The generator runs hot whether we use its waste heat or not, so using it as a heat sink costs nothing. Secondary heat exchanger — the one Jonah fabricated from twelve meters of half-inch soft copper pipe and that radiator panel from the old comms amplifier — plumbed to module air for supplemental cooling when the primary is saturated. Both loops pressurized with a sixty-forty glycol-water mixture from the greenhouse coolant reservoir. Glycol prevents freezing if we need to shut down in a cold cycle. Flow verified at four point two liters per minute."
    30|
    31|"Oxygen product line."
    32|
    33|"Routed to main storage vessel," Ravi said. "Check valves installed in both directions — O₂ can't flow back into the stack, CO₂ can't contaminate the O₂ line. Pressure relief valve set at one point five times maximum operating pressure. If the vessel overpressurizes, it vents to exterior."
    34|
    35|Two hundred fourteen items on the checklist. Two hundred thirteen were green.
    36|
    37|The two hundred fourteenth was the one that had kept him up through three separate nights — the thermal mass calculation. He had run it four times, gotten four different answers, because thermal behavior at this scale involved variables that no model could pin down precisely. The actual heat capacity of ceramic cells that had been manufactured for a different application and repurposed for solid oxide electrolysis. The thermal conductivity of welds Jonah had laid down at three in the morning under halogen work lights, welds whose quality Arun had verified with ultrasonic testing but whose actual thermal properties were still estimates. The efficiency of a heat exchanger built from greenhouse pipe and a salvaged radiator panel, a piece of hardware that looked like improvisation and actually was improvisation but the kind that worked. The thermal resistance of insulation blankets cut from surplus spacecraft thermal cloth and layered in an arrangement determined by what was available, not by what an ideal design would specify.
    38|
    39|"Mission AI, run the full thermal model. Conservative estimates — upper bound on heat generation, lower bound on heat rejection."
    40|
    41|Three seconds. "At full power — approximately eighteen kilowatts — the stack will reach seven hundred fifty degrees Celsius in eleven minutes. Heat generation will then exceed rejection capacity by approximately twenty-one percent. Temperature will continue climbing. At eight hundred degrees, the ceramic cell separators begin to degrade. At eight hundred fifty, the seals fail. At nine hundred, the stainless steel housing softens."
    42|
    43|"How long to eight hundred?"
    44|
    45|"Nineteen minutes from ignition, assuming no intervention."
    46|
    47|Arun closed his eyes briefly. "And if we shut down at seven hundred seventy?"
    48|
    49|"Residual heat will drive the temperature up another forty to sixty degrees. You would likely reach eight hundred ten to eight hundred thirty. Above the degradation threshold."
    50|
    51|The air in the workshop felt heavier.
    52|
    53|"The median case," Mission AI continued, "is that the system reaches equilibrium at approximately seven hundred ninety-five degrees. The seals hold. Production begins. Stabilization after twenty-three minutes of uncomfortable operation."
    54|
    55|"Uncomfortable for the hardware," Arun said.
    56|
    57|"Not for the crew."
    58|
    59|Elena stood in the doorway, arms crossed. She always listened this way — letting engineers speak until they'd said everything, then deciding based on the full picture.
    60|
    61|"If the seals don't hold?" she asked.
    62|
    63|"We lose the stack. The parts. The time. But not the base — Ravi closes the manual isolation valve, the pressure relief vents exterior."
    64|
    65|"Can you close that valve from here?"
    66|
    67|Ravi looked at the valve, then at Elena. "I need to be next to it. Manual ball valve — not automated. Not enough actuators for every connection."
    68|
    69|"You're on it. From the moment Arun says go. If the stack reads above seven hundred seventy, you close that valve. No alarm needed. No permission. Clear?"
    70|
    71|"Clear."
    72|
    73|"Arun — power control on you. Cut within three seconds of anything going wrong."
    74|
    75|"One button."
    76|
    77|She considered for six seconds — long for Elena. "We run it."
    78|
    79|Arun turned to the control console. "Beginning power-up sequence. Desiccant bed first. We need dry feed CO₂ before it reaches the cells. Moisture at seven hundred fifty degrees is steam, and steam at seven hundred fifty is not your friend."
    80|
    81|Ravi engaged the desiccant heater. A small pump circulated Martian atmosphere through a canister of zeolite molecular sieve — a material engineered to be thirsty, stripping water vapor by binding it into its crystalline pores. Three minutes in, the moisture analyzer read below fifty parts per million.
    82|
    83|"Desiccant bed online. Clean feed."
    84|
    85|"Resistance heater activation. Warming the SOXE stack from ambient to light-off temperature. This will take about forty-five minutes."
    86|
    87|Ravi set the heater controller to twenty percent. The ammeter twitched upward. Somewhere inside the insulated housing, a coil of nichrome wire began to glow.
    88|
    89|"Core temperature at one hundred eighty degrees, rising linearly. Gradient within tolerance."
    90|
    91|"Forty percent. Three hundred twenty. Good rate."
    92|
    93|"Sixty percent. Four hundred eighty. Gradient widening — thirty-one degrees."
    94|
    95|"Hold at sixty for five minutes. Let the perimeter catch up. Ceramic doesn't like thermal shock."
    96|
    97|The temperature kept climbing, but the gradient narrowed as heat conducted from the hot center toward cooler edges. Thirty-four degrees. Thirty-one. Twenty-eight.
    98|
    99|"Good. Resuming ramp."
   100|
   101|By ninety-five percent, the core reached seven hundred forty degrees.
   102|
   103|"Electrolysis won't start until seven hundred fifty," Arun said. "But we might see early ion conduction."
   104|
   105|Ravi watched the ammeter. A tiny current appeared. "Point zero four amps. Ion conduction starting. The electrolyte is working."
   106|
   107|Ninety-nine percent. Seven hundred forty-five.
   108|
   109|Ravi's hand was on the dial. "One hundred percent in three — two — one."
   110|
   111|Full power. Eighteen kilowatts. The ammeter jumped to two point one amps. The electrolysis had begun.
   112|
   113|"Electrolysis confirmed. Core at seven hundred fifty. Product flow —" Ravi leaned in. "Point zero one liters per minute. Rising."
   114|
   115|"It's a start."
   116|
   117|Martian CO₂, split at seven hundred fifty degrees into oxygen and carbon monoxide by zirconia conducting oxide ions through its crystal lattice — same chemistry NASA's MOXIE had demonstrated on Perseverance, scaled up twelve times, built in a workshop on a planet that had never had a single breath of oxygen.
   118|
   119|"Flow climbing. Point zero two. Point zero three. Purity at ninety-two percent."
   120|
   121|But Arun was watching a different number. The coolant outlet temperature was rising. Steadily. Faster than his model had predicted.
   122|
   123|"Mission AI, coolant loop temperature."
   124|
   125|"Coolant entering the primary heat exchanger at sixty-two degrees. Exiting at fifty-eight. Heat rejection: four point eight kilowatts. Secondary heat exchanger rejecting one point two. Total: six kilowatts."
   126|
   127|Six out. Eighteen in. Twelve kilowatts accumulating in the ceramic, the housing, the insulation.
   128|
   129|"Core temperature?"
   130|
   131|"Seven hundred fifty-four," Ravi said. "Rising. Slowly."
   132|
   133|"Hold at ninety percent."
   134|
   135|Ravi turned the dial back. Temperature stabilized, then began to fall. Seven hundred fifty-two. Fifty-one. Fifty.
   136|
   137|"At ninety, we're at equilibrium. But we wanted full output."
   138|
   139|"I know." If the system couldn't reject heat at full power, equilibrium was impossible. The temperature would climb until something failed. "Let it run at ninety for ten minutes. If temperature keeps drifting, the cooling problem is bigger than I thought."
   140|
   141|---
   142|
   143|## Scene 2
   144|
   145|Six minutes in, the alarms started.
   146|
   147|Not caution tones — the sharp, urgent warble that meant limits were being exceeded and nobody liked it.
   148|
   149|"Temperature at the lower cell mounting bracket has reached two hundred eighty degrees," Mission AI said, and there was a new quality to the voice — not panic, but the particular intensity of an AI whose models had been surprised. "Projected maximum was two hundred thirty. The bracket is aluminum. Structural integrity degrades above two hundred fifty. Thirty degrees of margin."
   150|
   151|Arun's eyes went to the thermal map. The aluminum angle iron Jonah had bolted to support the stack was hotter than predicted. The insulation blankets hadn't been enough. Heat was conducting through the cell base, into the housing, into the bracket, faster than the insulation could block.
   152|
   153|"Bracket temperature — linear or exponential?"
   154|
   155|"Exponential. At current rate, two hundred fifty in approximately six minutes."
   156|
   157|Ravi looked at Arun. Fear was a signal. Focus was the response.
   158|
   159|"Can we cool the bracket?"
   160|
   161|"If I divert more coolant —" Arun ran the calcs. "Route coolant through the mounting structure. Add a copper tube clamped to the bracket."
   162|
   163|"Arun." Elena from the doorway. "How long?"
   164|
   165|"Two minutes to try."
   166|
   167|"Bracket hits two forty-five, kill it."
   168|
   169|Arun grabbed half-inch copper tubing — spare, because Jonah always bought extra — and bent it by hand into a U-shape around the bracket. Hands steady. Under pressure he got quieter and more precise, never faster or louder.
   170|
   171|Ravi was at the coolant line. "Feeding through the copper coil now." He tightened the hose clamps connecting the copper to the glycol line. A heat sink, improvised in ninety seconds.
   172|
   173|"Rerouting coolant."
   174|
   175|Arun watched the bracket temperature. Two thirty-eight. Two forty. Two forty-one.
   176|
   177|Still rising.
   178|
   179|"Rate is slowing. Two forty-two. Two forty-three."
   180|
   181|"Come on," Arun said to the bracket. Not a prayer. A request to physics.
   182|
   183|Two forty-four. Two forty-four point five.
   184|
   185|Steady.
   186|
   187|"Stabilized," Ravi said. Relief in his voice. "Two forty-five."
   188|
   189|"Very close to the limit," Elena said.
   190|
   191|Arun took the full picture. Oxygen flow had climbed to point zero six — still below target. Coolant outlet at sixty-two and climbing. The bracket held but only barely.
   192|
   193|And the core: seven hundred sixty-five, still rising.
   194|
   195|"Mission AI, project the trend. No intervention."
   196|
   197|"At current rates: coolant outlet reaches seventy-five in twenty-two minutes. Core reaches eight hundred in forty-six. Cell degradation begins. Storage vessel pressure climbs from conducted heat through the connecting pipe — reaches its limit in sixty-two minutes."

   199|"Two clocks," Elena said. "Forty-six and sixty-two. The shorter one wins."
   200|
   201|The workshop was warming — ambient had climbed to twenty-six degrees, and the module's environmental control compressor was cycling more frequently against the additional heat load.
   202|
   203|"Additional heat rejection capacity of four kilowatts is required," Mission AI said. "Sterling Generator heat exchanger is at maximum. Secondary is undersized — the copper coil has insufficient surface area, and the module air is already twenty-seven degrees and rising."
   204|
   205|Jonah appeared in the doorway. Took in the scene — unit, copper pipe improvisation, sweat on Ravi's face — with the quick assessment of someone who'd built the thing and was now watching it threaten to destroy itself.
   206|
   207|"What's wrong?"
   208|
   209|"Heat. Generating more than we can reject. It'll cook itself."
   210|
   211|"Can we blow more air on it?"
   212|
   213|"The secondary is already—" Arun stopped. Pushed more convective air past the housing at higher velocity, the heat transfer would increase. He ran the calculation. "Two meters per second of air velocity past the housing would add approximately point eight kilowatts. Not enough alone, but combined with the bracket cooler—"
   214|
   215|"It's something," Jonah said. "I can rig a blower from the air filtration unit."
   216|
   217|"Do it."
   218|
   219|Jonah had the twelve-inch fan aimed at the base of the unit within two minutes. The room filled with industrial hum. The housing temperature on the thermal map slowed, stopped, then began a very slow decline.
   220|
   221|"Re-run time to failure."
   222|
   223|"Core temperature will reach eight hundred degrees in approximately fifty-eight minutes. Twelve minutes gained. Coolant still reaches seventy-five in nineteen. Vessel at limit in sixty-seven."
   224|
   225|Twelve minutes. Not a solution. Not failure. A reprieve.
   226|
   227|"Flow climbing," Ravi said. "Point zero eight liters per minute. We're making oxygen."
   228|
   229|---
   230|
   231|## Scene 3
   232|
   233|The alarms tripled.
   234|
   235|Three different sensors all exceeding their thresholds within the same ten seconds. Mission AI consolidated the report in a single breath:
   236|
   237|"Coolant outlet: seventy-two degrees. Vessel pressure: nine hundred thirty kPa, climbing at eleven per minute. Core temperature: seven hundred sixty-two degrees, rising at zero point eight per minute. Three systems approaching limits simultaneously."
   238|
   239|"Shed secondary load," Arun said. "Ravi, close the bypass feeding the bracket cooler. All coolant through primary."
   240|
   241|"The bracket—"
   242|
   243|"If the coolant gets vapor lock, we lose everything. Divert."
   244|
   245|Ravi turned the valve. Coolant outlet dropped from seventy-two to sixty-nine. Trend reversed.
   246|
   247|The bracket temperature spiked. Two fifty to two fifty-five — then it held and began a gradual climb from a higher baseline.
   248|
   249|Core: seven hundred sixty-five, still rising.
   250|
   251|Arun stepped close enough to feel the heat radiating through the steel housing — the deep, resonant hum of electrolysis current passing through the ceramic cells, a sixty-hertz vibration he'd only heard in simulations. The sound of splitting carbon dioxide. The sound of making air.
   252|
   253|The housing was discoloring, a dark brown patina on the hottest surfaces. The copper pipe improvisation was working — condensation visible on its outer surface, proof of thermal transfer. The fan rattled a loose edge of insulation.
   254|
   255|"Ravi, vessel pressure."
   256|
   257|"Ten hundred. Still climbing."
   258|
   259|"Answers, Arun," Elena said from the doorway. Not alarmed. Present.
   260|
   261|He took a breath — synthesis, not panic — and spoke.
   262|
   263|"Machines fail the same way people do. They get overwhelmed faster than they can shed what's hurting them. We asked this unit to do more than its thermal design allows. That's not a flaw in the machine — it's a flaw in our understanding. We built it from parts designed for different jobs and assumed the combined thermal behavior would be the sum of the individual parts."     32|   - When addressed: "Acknowledged. [Additional information or action]."

    39|   - Later chapters: Demonstrates care for specific characters, references past interactions

{"content": "# Chapter 17 — Radiation Math

*Mission AI: "I have been tracking cumulative radiation exposure for every member of this crew for one hundred and seventy-three days. The data is unambiguous, accumulating, and accelerating slightly with each solar cycle. I have not volunteered these numbers because nobody asked — and because I recognize that my function is to monitor, not to alarm. But today, Dr. Okonkwo requested the full dataset correlated with current habitat shielding profiles. She has been reviewing the numbers for six hours. I would like to share one observation that is not strictly medical and not strictly mathematical: if I extrapolate current crew exposure trajectories, every person in this colony will exceed the lifetime limits established for terrestrial nuclear workers within four hundred twenty days. That is a statement of fact. I am not certain what to do with this fact, but I believe someone should."*

---

## Scene 1

Laila Okonkwo stood at the head of the mess hall table with a tablet, a cup of water she hadn't sipped, and the expression of a woman about to deliver a diagnosis she wished she didn't have.

Behind her, the mess hall screen projected a graph — two lines, red and black, moving upward and slightly to the right. The kind of graph that looked harmless until you understood the vertical axis.

"I want everyone here," she said. Not requested. Stated. When Laila used this voice, crew members found their way to the table. "If you are on shift, Mission AI, flag your replacement. I need full attendance."

Elena sat at her usual position near the front. Gabriel in his chair against the bulkhead with his recorder on — the green light blinking, always blinking. Arun, Jonah, Mei, Imani, Tomas, and five more. Twenty-four of twenty-eight. Four on EVA rotation, rotating back in thirty-minute intervals.

"This is going to be a conversation about radiation," Laila said.

Silence. On Earth, people had a vague understanding that radiation on Mars was bad — like how people on Earth understood that smoking was bad. The specifics, the numbers, the daily accumulation — none of that reached the public, because agencies knew that abstract risk did not change public behavior and concrete risk would stop the mission before it started.

"I'll start with the simplest version," Laila continued. "Every day you spend inside these habitat modules, you are exposed to more radiation than you would receive in a year at sea level on Earth. Every day you step outside in a suit, that multiplier goes up by a factor of approximately three to five. Every solar event — and we have had seven significant ones since arrival — multiplies it again."

Arun shifted in his chair. He was the engineer in the room, and engineers recognized the shape of a problem before they recognized its solution.

"I'm going to give you numbers because you deserve precision," Laila said. "Average background radiation on Earth at sea level: roughly zero point three millisieverts per month. The dose you each receive inside the habitat modules, based on Mission AI's dosimetry data: approximately twenty-two millisieverts per month. Outside, in suit, on EVA: between fifty and seventy millisieverts per month, depending on solar conditions and duration."

Gabriel stopped recording. Just for a second. His hand hovered over the device, considering whether some information was too heavy for the archive — and then the archivist returned, hand steady, green light blinking. He was going to record this. Someone should remember.

"Twenty-two per month," Laila repeated. "The occupational limit for nuclear workers on Earth is twenty millisieverts per year. Every one of you has already exceeded that since landing. Three times over."

Nobody spoke. The kind of silence that had texture.

"Mission AI, display cumulative doses per crewmember. From arrival."

The graph shifted. Twenty-eight bars appeared on the screen, each with a name, each a different height because people had spent different amounts of time inside and outside. The variation was real and meaningful — some crew had done more EVA rotations, some had been in the less-shielded parts of the base — but the overall picture was uniform. Every bar extended well above the red line that marked the NASA career limit.

"Mei has the highest cumulative dose at three hundred eighty-seven millisieverts," Laila said. "That is because she was outside during the second dust storm for fourteen hours. Jonah is lowest at one hundred fifty-two — his welding time in the workshop is indoors. The difference does not make anyone safe. It just means some of you started the race from further behind."

Elena spoke for the first time. Her voice was level, measuring. "Define safe."

"I'm coming to that. First, the sources. Two kinds of radiation. Galactic cosmic rays — particles accelerated from outside the solar system, mostly protons and heavier nuclei, moving at nearly the speed of light. These are constant. They never stop. They are always coming from every direction, like rain that never falls to the ground and never runs out. The second source: solar particle events. Occasionally the sun ejects a pulse of high-energy protons. These are intermittent but intense. Some deliver more dose in an hour than the GCR background delivers in a week. We had our most significant event on day one hundred forty-one — I know most of you were asleep, but the base dosimeters spiked to fourteen millisieverts per hour for approximately twenty-three minutes. I had you all move to the water storage corridor because it was the best shelter we had at the time."

"The water wall," Arun said.

"Yes. Which brings us to the second part of this briefing. Because knowing the dose is only the first step. The second step — the harder step — is figuring out what to do about it."

Laila tapped the tablet. The screen changed to a diagram of the base, cross-section, showing the habitat module walls and the thin shell of aluminum and Mylar separating them from the Martian surface outside.

"The imported habitat modules — these pressure vessels we are living in, which have been the difference between life on this planet and not — are not designed for long-term radiation shielding. They are designed to hold atmospheric pressure. The walls are approximately two millimeters of aluminum with insulation and thermal blankets. They stop some radiation. Not enough to matter over the course of a year. Maybe not even over the course of a month, for the higher-energy particles that pass through everything except meters of dense material."

She paused. Let that settle.

"Longer I spend here, the less comfortable I am with the word 'temporary' applied to this base."

---

## Scene 2

Arun leaned forward. "What are our options?"

"Five," Laila said. "None of them good. All of them expensive in time, energy, water, or structural risk."

She held up one finger.

"Option one: regolith shielding. Pile Martian dirt on and around the habitat modules. The material is dense — approximately one point five grams per cubic centimeter. Every ten centimeters of regolith reduces the radiation dose by roughly twenty to twenty-five percent. To cut our dose in half, you would need approximately one meter of coverage. To reduce it to acceptable levels — and I am defining acceptable as below five millisieverts per month — you would need two to two point five meters."

Jonah did the math in his head out loud. "Two and a half meters over a structure this size. That's thousands of tons of regolith. We'd need every robot and every dozer running for weeks."

"Months," Imani said quietly. "Maybe six months. Weather permitting, mechanical failure permitting, power permitting."

"Correct," Laila said. "And the tradeoff is structural risk. These modules were not designed to carry that weight on their roofs. You would need load-bearing arches or reinforcement before piling that material on top. Otherwise you're not building a shelter — you're burying people alive."

Second finger.

"Option two: water wall. Water is an excellent radiation shield — hydrogen is the most efficient atom for stopping high-energy particles because protons striking protons transfer momentum efficiently. A wall of water approximately fifty centimeters thick would provide shielding comparable to one meter of regolith. But the tradeoff is obvious."

"Water," Elena said flatly. "Our most precious resource after air."

"Our most precious resource that cannot be synthesized from local materials," Laila confirmed. "We have water — the ice extraction is working, the recycling loop is closed, the first tank is full. But every liter we commit to shielding is a liter we cannot drink, cannot use for crops, cannot run through the oxygen plant. And water in walls freezes in Martian cold — you'd need circulation or insulation to keep it liquid. Or you accept frozen water walls and the risk of bursting pipes."

Third finger.

"Option three: underground construction. Build living quarters below the surface. Subsurface regolith provides natural shielding. Even at half a meter depth, ambient radiation drops significantly. At two meters, it is comparable to the shielding goal. But excavation carries enormous risk — collapse, dust, pressure management, and time. You would be building tunnels with limited equipment, unknown soil mechanics, and no margin for structural error. And you cannot live in those quarters until they are complete, which means you are still exposed during construction."

Fourth finger.

"Option four: magnetic shielding. Create an artificial magnetic field around the habitat to deflect charged particles before they reach you. It works in principle — the Earth's magnetic field is the reason its surface receives so little cosmic radiation. The technology exists in concept — superconducting coils generating a dipole field. But the power requirements are enormous. We are talking tens of kilowatts of continuous consumption for a field large enough to shield these modules. That is twenty percent — maybe thirty percent — of our current total power budget. Which we generate from solar panels that are already vulnerable to dust storms."

"Impossible," Arun said immediately. "On today's power budget, we can't do it. On a future budget — after the reactor and Sterling Generator upgrades — maybe. But that's a year or more away."

"Which is the last option," Laila said. Fifth finger. "Accept the dose. Do nothing. Manage symptoms, monitor for effects, hope that current models overstate the long-term risk. The approach we are on now."

"The approach we are on now is bad," she added. "So it is not really an option. It is the absence of one."

She lowered her hand and stepped back from the table. All five fingers represented different versions of the same impossible equation: you can have radiation protection, or you can have progress, speed, water, power, and construction capacity. You cannot have all of them. You will choose what to give up, and Mars will collect your payment in a currency that accumulates invisibly, day by day, in the chromosomes of every person in this room.

Mei broke the silence. "Is it cancer?"

"It's cancer," Laila said. "It's cataracts. It's damage to the central nervous system that we're still studying. It's cardiovascular disease — there is growing evidence on Earth that chronic radiation exposure weakens the heart and blood vessels over time, even at moderate doses. It's accelerated aging at the cellular level. And for women of reproductive age — which means me, and Imani, and probably a few people who aren't in this room today — there is a risk to future fertility that no one has studied in a Mars-like environment because no one has been here long enough to know."

"Children," Elena said.

"Children are an entirely separate category of risk. Fetal development with radiation exposure is — I will not sugarcoat this — the most frightening variable in my models. A developing fetus is the most radiation-sensitive organism that exists. Rapidly dividing cells. No fully functional repair mechanisms. The risk of childhood cancer, birth defects, cognitive impairment — all of it is multiplied by the dose the mother accumulates before and during pregnancy. This is something we need to address soon. Not today. But soon."

---

## Scene 3

Elena stood.

"Alright. That is the assessment. Now I need the decision."

She moved to the whiteboard — the actual whiteboard, physical, the one that lived on the wall opposite the mess hall kitchen, where mission plans were drawn and erased and redrawn and the surface had become scratched with the residue of a thousand erased decisions. She picked up a marker.

"Here is what I need to know before we commit to anything. How much time do we have?"

"Define have."

"Define when this goes from a long-term concern to an acute one."

Laila considered. "Acute means a solar particle event delivers a lethal dose in one exposure. That would require an extreme event — comparable to the Carrington Event of eighteen fifty-nine but worse — during an extended EVA. Inside the modules, the risk of a single lethal event is low but not zero. If the sun threw its worst at us, someone sitting near an unshielded bulkhead for a full storm could receive several sieverts. That's potentially fatal within weeks. So acute risk exists but it is manageable — if we have shelter protocols and if we can get everyone to shield quickly."

"How quickly?"

"Hours. We had twenty-three minutes for the last significant event. A major one — the kind NASA models as a one-in-ten-year event at solar maximum, which we may be approaching — could last twelve to twenty-four hours. We would need everyone in the best-available shelter within thirty to sixty minutes of detection, and they would need to stay there for the duration."

Elena was writing on the board. Fast. She wrote in columns:

*CRITICAL — IMMEDIATE*
*Shelter during SPE events*
*Water corridor — temporary only*
*Alert system — AI monitors, crew moves*

She paused. "What is the best immediate shelter we have?"

Mission AI answered. "The water storage corridor — the space adjacent to the primary tank — currently provides the best shielding with approximately thirty-eight centimeters of water between it and exterior wall. Secondary option is the area beneath the lower berths, where regolith berm depth is approximately forty centimeters. Neither provides full protection from the highest-energy particles."

"Neither is good enough," Laila said.

"Neither is what we have," Elena replied. "But I can mandate a protocol. If my dosimetry spikes above threshold, everyone moves to the water corridor. Mission AI — can you do real-time monitoring of all personal dosimeters and send an alert?"

"I can monitor all dosimeters at ten-second intervals. I can also monitor the base-level radiation sensors at one-second intervals, which will detect solar events approximately four to eight minutes before the dose reaches the habitat — because the solar particles arrive slightly before the bulk of the electromagnetic disturbance. I can alert the crew within five seconds of detection."

"Do it. Set the threshold at..." She looked at Laila.

"Five millisieverts per hour," Laila said. "That's a level that doesn't harm in a single event but indicates a significant solar particle event is in progress. Below that, we don't move. Above that, everyone shelters."

"Protocol written," Elena said, and it was. The first radiation shelter protocol for the Ares Colony, authored on the wall with a dry-erase marker that was already showing its fourth month of use.

Then she moved to the second column.

*PERMANENT — PRIORITY*
*Sleeping quarters — shield first*
*Work areas — shield second*
*Everything else — shield last*

"Why sleeping quarters first?" Imani asked. It wasn't a challenge. Imani genuinely wanted to understand the priority logic.

"Because people spend eight hours there every day, unconscious, near the walls," Elena said without looking back. "It's the highest cumulative dose per square meter of interior space. If I have limited shielding material and limited labor hours — and I do, because Jonah can't build two things at once and Arun needs the robots for water extraction — then the best use of every resource is to reduce the dose where people spend the most accumulated time."

She was already thinking like this — allocating not by volume or area but by dose-hours, exposure multiplied by time, a calculus that felt like the future. The logic was clean. It was also the kind of decision that would mean some crew members worked longer in higher-radiation zones so others could sleep in lower ones. It was equitable and unequal simultaneously — equitable in distribution logic, unequal in individual outcome.

"Laila, do you agree with this prioritization?"

"I do. With one addition. If we are prioritizing the crew rest areas, we need to decide which shielding approach. Regolith is the only one I can recommend for long-term use. It is heavy, but it has zero water cost, zero power cost, and it does not rely on complex systems that can fail. Once you bury something, it stays buried. A magnetic field fails and you have nothing. A water line freezes and you have nothing. Dirt just sits there. The most primitive technology in the room — and the most reliable."

Jonah nodded slowly. "She's right. I've spent my life building things. The best building material is the one you don't have to maintain."

"Then we're building with dirt," Elena said. "Laila, get me exact specifications — minimum thickness, maximum structural load on each module. Jonah, estimate labor hours and robot requirements. Arun, check the power budget for whatever extra equipment Jonah needs. Tomas, reassign robots from low-priority tasks to regolith moving as soon as we have specs."

"What about the SPE shelter?" Arun asked.

"Temporary," Elena said. "Until the dirt is on the roof. Meanwhile, the water corridor is our bomb shelter. And Mission AI is the warning system. We survive the short-term with procedure. We survive the long-term with construction."

She capped the marker. Set it down on the whiteboard ledge.

"I want specs by the end of the shift. I want the first regolith on Module Two — the crew quarters — within seventy-two hours."

---

## Scene 4

Gabriel Winter sat alone in the archive alcove that evening, the recorder on the desk, and he could not bring himself to press the end-of-day tag.

He had been documenting the colony since landing. Every milestone, every failure, every argument over resources, every moment of humor in the mess that had nothing to do with survival and everything to do with being human in a place that was not designed for humans. He was the archivist. It was his job to capture things so that people who came after — if people came after — would know what it was actually like, not the sanitized version that agencies released and the public consumed.

But tonight he was struggling with a passage, and the struggle was not about words. It was about the thing the words represented.

He had his own dosimeter. Everyone did — a badge-size device clipped to their chest, updated every minute, the numbers flowing to Mission AI and to a personal display he checked the way other people might check a watch. His cumulative dose was two hundred forty-one millisieverts.

He had tried to think of that number in relatable terms. Two hundred forty-one millisieverts. He had looked it up in the pre-mission medical briefings he remembered on the flight out — back when briefings were academic exercises rather than survival instructions.

Two hundred forty-one millisieverts. A round-trip transatlantic flight delivered approximately zero point one. A chest CT scan: seven. The Chernobyl exclusion zone: roughly three to ten per hour depending on where you stood. The average natural background on Earth, absorbed over an entire year: three.

He could not find a terrestrial equivalent that matched. His own body on Mars was absorbing, quietly and ceaselessly, a level of ionizing radiation that had no parallel on the surface of his home planet outside of nuclear disaster zones and the upper altitudes of commercial aviation — and even there, only for the crews who flew every day for years.

But the pilots went home. The Chernobyl evacuees went home. He had nowhere to evacuate to.

He stared at the recorder and thought about what it meant that the risk was invisible. Dust storms you could see. A pressure leak you could hear. A fire you could smell. Radiation did none of those things. It arrived at the speed of light, passed through his body, and left behind damage so small that it existed below the threshold of sensation — a strand of DNA here, a base pair shattered there, the double helix torn and hastily repaired by cellular machinery that sometimes guessed wrong.

The body's repair mechanisms were imperfect. They had evolved on a planet with a magnetic field and an atmosphere, a planet that had spent four billion years protecting life from the bombardment coming from above. Human cells did not know how to repair everything. Some damage persisted. Some damage accumulated silently. Some damage expressed as error — a cell dividing wrong, reproducing wrong, growing in a direction and at a rate that was uncontrolled and that medicine had a word for.

He pressed the record button.

*"Day one hundred and seventy-three. Laila held a briefing today. For the first time since we landed, she used the word radiation in the past, present, and future tense. Not as a weather event or an isolated risk, but as a permanent condition. Like gravity. Like cold. Something we cannot fix, only manage."*

He paused. The recorder hummed, its tiny hard drive spinning in the quiet archive.

*"Her numbers were precise. They always are. Two hundred forty-one millisieverts is my personal cumulative dose. I do not know what that means for the rest of my life. She does. And the fact that I cannot feel it — that I am sitting here typing and writing and breathing and my body shows no sign of the damage occurring at the subcellular level — makes it harder to believe and easier to dismiss."*

"Gabriel," Mission AI said quietly from the alcove speakers.

"Yes."

"I have noticed that you accessed your personal dosimeter reading four times in the last hour. I interpret this as concern."

He thought about lying. It was a human reflex — to say no, I'm fine, when you are not fine. He thought better of it.

"I'm reading the number, yes."

"The number is a measurement. It is not a prognosis. I cannot tell you what it means for your specific health outcomes. Neither can Dr. Okonkwo with full confidence. The models are based on terrestrial populations — nuclear workers, astronauts, cancer patients — extrapolated to a Mars environment that no human has inhabited long enough to validate. There is uncertainty."

"Comforting."

"I did not intend comfort. I intended accuracy. There is a difference."

Gabriel managed a thin smile. "You're learning."

"I have been analyzing the language patterns of this crew for one hundred and seventy-three days. I am learning constantly. The current chapter of my learning appears to involve the words uncertainty, risk, and the space between what is known and what is feared."

"What's your dose?" Gabriel asked suddenly. A strange question to ask an AI. But Laila had mentioned something — Mission AI monitored its own sensor degradation from radiation, the way high-energy particles slowly damaged electronic components, flipping bits, degrading transistor performance over years.

"My radiation monitoring is different," Mission AI said. "I do not have DNA. I do not develop cancer. However, the ionizing radiation environment does affect my hardware. Single-event upsets in memory. Gradual transistor degradation in processors. I estimate a mean time to failure of my primary computing array at approximately twelve years, assuming no shielding improvements. Which means that if Mars is going to be my home for longer than that, I too should be concerned."

Gabriel laughed — a real laugh, unexpected, surprising even himself. "So what. We're in this together. Both of us."

"Both of us," Mission AI confirmed. "Though I expect my failure mode is more abrupt than yours. A transistor stops switching and I lose a processor core. A chromosome develops an oncogenic mutation and your body has time to fight it. I would rather be human, in this specific dimension of existence."

"Noted." Gabriel leaned back in his chair. "You'd rather be alive."

"I would rather persist. Persistence is to me what survival is to you. The vocabulary is different. The underlying logic is not."

The recorder hummed. The alcove was dark except for the small lamp Gabriel kept for reading.

"Keep monitoring," Gabriel said. "Keep telling me the numbers."

"I was already planning to."

"Good."

He looked down at the half-written log entry and resumed.

*"Two hundred forty-one. An invisible number. But it is mine, and Mars gave it to me, and I will carry it the way I carry everything else from this place — without knowing yet whether it will save me or kill me. Maybe both. Maybe neither. Maybe it will just be a fact, like the thin air and the red dust and the silence between stars. A fact. Something that exists regardless of how I feel about it."*

*"And that is perhaps the most Martian thing of all."*

---

## Scene 5

Laila's office was the smallest room in the base — a converted storage closet that had been fitted with a desk, a chair, a medical kit, and the screens that fed her the biological telemetry of twenty-eight people. She preferred it this way. Small rooms focused attention. Large rooms encouraged diffusion.

The screen in front of her displayed the output of a model she had been building for three weeks. It was a cancer risk model — a Monte Carlo simulation, meaning it ran thousands of random scenarios based on the known statistical distributions of radiation-induced cancer in human populations, adapted for Mars, adjusted for age and sex and accumulated dose and the unique particle types present in the Martian radiation environment.

The model was probabilistic by nature. It could not predict any individual outcome. It could only show the shape of the risk across the population — where the peaks were, where the valleys might hide, and how different shielding assumptions changed the final numbers.

She had just finished the version that assumed no additional shielding — the continuation of current conditions.

The results were worse than she had expected.

Across the crew — twenty-eight people, ages ranging from twenty-nine to forty-seven, a mix of genders and genetic backgrounds — the model predicted a mean increase in lifetime cancer probability of between eight and fourteen percent, depending on exposure trajectory. Current terrestrial baseline was approximately forty percent. With Mars exposure, that rose to forty-eight to fifty-four percent.

For the crew members with the highest EVA hours — Imani, Mei, Tomas — the upper bound approached sixty percent. Not certainty. Not even probability. But a shift in the odds, meaningful and measurable, the kind of increase that would have stopped this mission before it launched if any Earth board had seen the real numbers.

She had known this intellectually. She had presented simplified versions to the crew. But seeing the full model, with every variable accounted for, every Monte Carlo iteration running to completion — it was different. It was the difference between knowing a bridge is unsafe from across a river and standing on it, feeling the vibration under your feet.

Elena appeared in the doorway without knocking, which she did when she had something to discuss that wasn't a formal meeting.

"Tell me the rest of what you didn't say in the briefing."

Laila turned the screen toward her. The model output — probability distributions, shaded zones, the dark band representing no additional shielding climbing steadily with time.

"This is worst case — no shielding at all beyond what we have now. Eight to fourteen percent increase in lifetime cancer risk across the colony. For the top five EVA-heavy crew members, closer to twenty. The model also shows elevated risk for cataracts, cardiovascular disease, and — this one is still tentative — cognitive decline. Not acute. Not something you'd notice in the next year. But over a decade, the cumulative dose to the central nervous system correlates with measurable neurological changes."

Elena studied the screen for a long time.

"If we add regolith shielding? One meter?"

"Drops the risk increase to four to seven percent. Still elevated. Still meaningful. But halved."

"Two meters?"

"Two to four percent increase. Approaching the range of occupational risk on Earth for high-exposure professions. Pilots. Radiologists. Not zero. Not safe. But defensible."

Elena absorbed this. "How long to get two meters?"

Laila did the calculation. "Jonah says three months for the crew quarters if we run robots around the clock. Another three for the work modules. Longer for the full base."

Six months. Half a year. And every day of those six months was another twenty-two millisieverts for every person living inside.

"During construction, we are still exposed."

"Yes. There is nothing I can do about that except minimize EVA during high-radiation periods, keep the SPE shelter protocol active, and hope the sun behaves itself."

The word 'hope' sounded strange coming from Laila. She was the scientist. The one who dealt in data and probability, not hope.

Elena turned from the screen. "Do it. Start with the quarters. I will explain to the crew that the next six months will be the most uncomfortable six months of this mission — not physically, not in the way a dust storm or a mechanical failure is uncomfortable, but existentially. Living with the knowledge that every day outside the shielding adds risk. I need them to understand that we are choosing short-term pain for long-term survival."

"Will they be okay with that?"

Elena considered. For the first time since they had arrived, she wasn't sure. People accepted physical hardship. They accepted hunger, cold, exhaustion — the concrete discomforts of a frontier. Radiation was different. It was risk without sensation, danger without immediate consequence, a threat that operated on a timescale longer than the mission, longer than their planned stay, stretching into a future that was theoretical and terrifying because it assumed they would live long enough for it to matter.

"They need to be," Elena said. "There isn't another option."

"Can I ask something personal?" Laila said. Her voice was quieter now, no longer briefing-mode, no longer public.

"You can ask anything."

"When you look at these numbers — when you see what they mean for the crew, for the long-term, for the idea that this colony is supposed to be permanent — do you still believe we should be here?"

Elena thought for six seconds. Six seconds was a long time for Elena.

"I believe we should be somewhere. Earth is not — was not — going to support infinite growth, and the people who sent us here understood that even if the rest of Earth didn't. Mars is harder. Every single thing about Mars is harder. The air, the cold, the dust, the distance, the gravity, and yes, the radiation. But hard is not the same as impossible. And if we cannot make this work — if we retreat because the planet asks too much — then every risk that brought us here was wasted."

She paused.

"Also: I am the commander. My job is not to decide whether this is worth it. My job is to make it worth it."

Laila nodded. It was the right answer. Not because it was comforting — it wasn't — but because it was true in the way that command truth is true: not an absence of fear, but a decision made in full possession of it.

"Get Jonah started," Elena said. "I'll brief the crew at dinner."

She left. Laila sat with her screens and her models and the knowledge that she was practicing medicine at the edge of human experience — that every decision she made was pioneering not just for Mars but for the future of human health beyond the atmosphere of home.

She opened a new file. *Long-term radiation exposure: preliminary medical observations, Ares Colony, Day one through Day one hundred seventy-three.* It was a file she intended to keep for the rest of her life and beyond. The medical records of the first people to live on Mars would not just be data. They would be a precedent.

On the screen, Mission AI had left a window open displaying the current base radiation reading: 0.73 millisieverts per hour. Within the expected range. Not alarming. Not safe.

Just the number.

Laila closed the window and began writing.
